# Harrowgate Community Trust

## Six-Month Programme Plan: January–June 2026

**Prepared for:** the Board of Trustees  
**Date:** January 2026, revised against the 12 January 2026 update pack  
**Programming budget:** £60,000  
**Status:** for approval

---

## 1. Summary

This is a portfolio plan, not a single bet. It protects the session that is working, tests the transport explanation on the one evening when transport has changed, uses the east hall only after it is certified, and keeps a small, honest test of the one slot on which the trust has no local evidence.

1. **Protect the Saturday family workshop.** It is the only session that grew in 2025 (+21%). It runs every Saturday. Family-fund childcare is requested for 20 of the 26 Saturdays, within the reduced £4,000 fund.
2. **Test transport on Fridays.** The town council's late bus starts on Friday 6 February and leaves the square at 21:15. The Friday series ends at 20:30, leaving 45 minutes to reach it. This is a bounded test with a stop rule, not a six-month commitment.
3. **Use the east hall after the certificate.** There is no public event in the east hall before the commissioning certificate. A soft opening follows the certificate, then a four-week textile exhibition from 11 April, subject to two weeks of environmental monitoring and curator sign-off.
4. **Test Sunday afternoon small.** Three salons, with a stop rule, because 12% of survey respondents prefer Sunday afternoon and the trust has no local evidence either way.
5. **Hold a reserve.** The plan commits £56,375, including a 10% contingency, and leaves £3,625 as a board reserve within the £60,000 ceiling.

|---|---:|
| Tuesday Craft Group sessions | 25 |
| Thursday Film Club screenings | 12 |
| Saturday Family Workshops | 26 |
| Friday evening events | 20 |
| East hall public workshops | 10 |
| Sunday afternoon salons | 3 |
| Community-group minibus visits | 4 |
| Saturday family minibus runs | 2 |
| **Direct programme** | **£51,250** |
| **Contingency (10%)** | **£5,125** |
| **Total committed** | **£56,375** |
| **Board reserve to £60,000** | **£3,625** |

**Key dates**

| Date | Milestone |
|---|---|
| Fri 6 Feb | Friday late bus starts; Friday evening series launches |
| Mon 9–Fri 27 Feb | East hall HVAC works; no public events in the east hall |
| Sat 28 Feb | Commissioning scheduled |
| Mon 2 Mar | Commissioning certificate check; no east hall booking before this |
| Sat 14 Mar | East hall soft opening, subject to the certificate |
| Mon 16 Mar–Fri 3 Apr | Exhibition install and environmental monitoring; curator sign-off by 3 April |
| Sat 11 Apr–Sat 9 May | *Threads of Harrowgate* exhibition |
| Thu 30 Apr | Transport data pack to the town council |
| Early May | Friday series decision for June |
| Sat 20 Jun | Harrowgate Open House |
| Fri 10 Jul | Final evaluation report to the board |

---

## 2. What the evidence says

### 2.1 Attendance: a modest overall decline, but a clear mix shift

The attendance CSV is the only continuous quantitative series in the pack. It shows a 3.2% fall in total attendances in 2025 (1,030 to 997), but the fall is not uniform.

| Session | 2024 average per month | 2025 average per month | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Tuesday Craft Group | 33.9 | 29.2 | −14% |
| Thursday Film Club | 20.7 | 16.2 | −22% |
| Saturday Family Workshop | 31.2 | 37.8 | +21% |
| **All sessions** | **85.8** | **83.1** | **−3.2%** |

Two further points matter:

- **The decline is concentrated in the second half of 2025.** January–June 2025 totalled 523 attendances against 515 in the same months of 2024 (+1.6%). July–December 2025 totalled 474 against 515 (−8.0%).
- **The family workshop grew when childcare was added.** Its 2024 average was 26.9 in January–August and 42.3 in October–December, after the childcare pilot began. The 2025 January–June average was 39.7.

The implication is not that the whole programme is failing. It is that the weekday and evening offer is losing people while the Saturday family offer is working. The plan therefore protects the family workshop and treats the weekday and evening offer as the part that needs testing.

### 2.2 The survey: transport is the strongest signal, but it is a stated preference

The 2025 member survey had 240 responses from 610 members (39%). It was self-selected, and the survey volunteer's method note is explicit: the evening-transport figure is a stated preference; people were asked to imagine a bus, not tested on whether they would come, and were not asked what they would pay.

| Survey question | Result |
|---|---|
| What stops you attending more often? (up to two) | Transport 61%; programme does not appeal 34%; cost 29%; caring responsibilities 27%; other 11% |
| Would you attend an evening event if transport were available? | Yes 44%; maybe 21%; no 35% |
| Which time suits you best? | Saturday morning 38%; weekday morning 24%; weekday evening 18%; Sunday afternoon 12%; no preference 8% |
| Would free childcare make it easier to attend? | Yes 27%, of whom 81% are members with children under 12 |

Transport is the strongest signal, but 35% say they would not come even with transport, and the 44% is not a forecast. The time-preference data is more useful for scheduling: Saturday morning is the strongest preference, weekday morning is next, and Sunday afternoon is the weakest. That is why the plan is weighted to Saturday morning and daytime, and why the Sunday test is deliberately small.

The survey also explains why the plan does not put money into a digital campaign. Cost (29%) and caring responsibilities (27%) are addressed through pay-what-you-can pricing, free exhibition entry and the childcare offer, not through a separate subsidy line.

### 2.3 Prior interventions: remove friction, don't just change content

- **2023 Friday evening film pilot.** Three screenings drew 37, 23 and 19 people. Booking data shows 60 seats were reserved for the first night and 48 for the second, so attendance was 62% and 48% of reservations. The series was cancelled. The programmer's note says people liked the films but could not get home; the staff interviews corroborate the 18:40 last bus and a £14 return taxi. The mean attendance was 26.3, and the fall from first to third night was 49%. This is a strong hypothesis, not proof: only three nights, no written evaluation, the room is not recorded, and there is no ticket income data.
- **2024 Saturday childcare pilot.** Attendance rose from an average of 27 in the first eight months of 2024 to 42 in the last four. The family fund paid £180 per session. Staff report that families stayed for the café and some began attending the Tuesday Craft Group. This is the clearest evidence in the pack that removing a practical barrier works.
- **2024 website and ticketing migration.** Web traffic rose 12%, but there is no evidence that this changed attendance; the decline continued through 2025. Digital spend is therefore not treated as a solution.
- **2022 outreach van.** It averaged 11 attendances per visit, was withdrawn when its grant ended, and left no written evaluation. Staff remember it as "worthwhile but not a substitute for the building". It is not a model to scale.

### 2.4 Building, staffing and money are hard boundaries

- The east hall has not been climate-controlled since the HVAC unit failed in January 2025. The 2019 "climate-controlled" description is not relied on. The west hall and workshop room are usable throughout; the basement is damp and unsuitable for sensitive material.
- The pack contains no temperature or humidity readings for the east hall, before or after repair; no blackout data for either hall; and no floor-loading, rigging or fire-safety data. The 120 seated / 180 standing figures are audience capacities, not load ratings. Heavy or suspended work needs a building officer's check.
- The trust has 2.0 FTE permanent staff (director, programmer), 0.5 FTE administrator and eight volunteers. Evening events require two staff present; childcare requires two qualified workers; volunteers are not asked to work alone after 18:00.
- Events may run until 23:00, and the building must be empty by 23:30.
- The programming budget covers artists, materials, marketing, bought-in staff hours and event costs. Building repairs are funded separately. The family fund is separate and capped at £4,000 for this period.

The plan is built around these boundaries: no east hall public events before the certificate; no new Thursday evening series; Friday events end at 20:30; sessional staff cover evenings; no new permanent posts.

### 2.5 What the January updates changed

| Update | What it says | What I had assumed from the seed pack | What the plan now does |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Family fund** | £4,000 for January–June 2026, not the £9,000 in the seed pack. At £180 per Saturday, the fund covers at most 22 sessions (£3,960), leaving four Saturdays without family-fund support. The fund may also be used for other family support. From April, childcare must be advertised as "supported by the family fund" and cannot be described as permanently free. | I had assumed weekly childcare (26 × £180 = £4,680) was affordable. It is not. | I request 20 sessions (£3,600) and hold £400 for other family support, so six Saturdays run without childcare. The Family Workshop still runs every Saturday. From April, all childcare publicity uses the required wording. If the trustees confirm 22 sessions, I restore childcare on 14 February and 28 March. |
| **East hall repair** | The council has approved the capital grant. The contractor works 9–27 February; commissioning is 28 February; the hall is expected to be usable for sensitive material from 1 March. The building officer says this is a plan, not a guarantee, and nothing should be booked before the commissioning certificate. The repair is capital and outside the £60,000. | I had treated the east hall as uncertain and unavailable for the whole period. | I plan a certificate check on 2 March, a soft opening on 14 March and a textile exhibition from 11 April, subject to two weeks of monitoring and curator sign-off. No east hall events are scheduled in January or February. The £18,000 repair is excluded from the programming budget. |
| **Transport** | The town council has approved a Friday late bus pilot from 6 February 2026. The last service from the square will leave at 21:15 instead of 18:40. It is funded for six months, covers Fridays only, and will be reviewed in July; the council will look at ridership after three months. There is no change to Saturday or Sunday service and no extra service on other weekdays. | I had assumed no viable evening offer, because the 2023 pilot ran with an 18:40 last bus. | I plan a Friday series ending at 20:30, and no new Thursday evening series. I have not assumed late transport on any other day. The Friday series is a test, not a core commitment, and a data pack goes to the council by 30 April. |
| **Website** | The migration is complete, the old domain redirects, online booking works and the newsletter open rate is stable. The update says it has no effect on the programme plan. | I had treated the 2024 traffic increase as a possible attendance lever, but the evidence did not support that. | No programme money is allocated to the website or a digital campaign, and I have not assumed the 2024 traffic increase will translate into attendance. |

Two earlier project notes are now stale and are not relied on. The note "East hall is climate-controlled" comes from the 2019 building survey; the HVAC failed in January 2025 and the hall is uncontrolled until the repair is commissioned. The note "Members want evening events" reads the 44% "yes" without the 35% "no" or the survey volunteer's warning that the question was hypothetical. Both are corrected in this plan.

---

## 5. Rationale

### 5.1 Evidence I relied on

I treated the attendance CSV as the primary quantitative evidence because it is the only continuous series in the pack. It shows a 3.2% fall in total attendances in 2025, but the fall is not uniform: January–June 2025 was 1.6% above the same months of 2024, while July–December was 8.0% below; Craft Group fell 14%, the Film Club fell 22%, and the Saturday Family Workshop grew 21%. That is why the plan protects the Family Workshop and treats the weekday and evening offer as the part that needs testing, rather than assuming a general collapse.

I used the 2025 member survey as a signal, not a forecast. Transport is the most cited barrier at 61%, but the 44% who said they would attend an evening event if transport were available were answering a hypothetical question; the survey volunteer explicitly warns that the trust did not test whether they would actually come or what they would pay. I therefore did not plan on 44% turning up. I used the time-preference data — Saturday morning 38%, weekday morning 24%, weekday evening 18%, Sunday afternoon 12% — to weight the programme toward Saturday morning and daytime, and to keep the Sunday test small. Cost (29%) and caring responsibilities (27%) are addressed through pay-what-you-can pricing, free exhibition entry and the childcare offer, rather than through a separate subsidy line.

I used the prior interventions as natural experiments. The 2023 Friday films drew 37, 23 and 19 people, with 60 and 48 seats reserved, and were cancelled; the programmer's note and the staff interviews point to the journey home, with the 18:40 last bus and the £14 return taxi. That is a strong hypothesis, not proof, so the Friday series is a test with a stop rule. The 2024 childcare pilot, where the Family Workshop average rose from 27 to 42, is the clearest evidence that removing a practical barrier works; it is why childcare remains central to the family offer, within the reduced fund. The 2024 website migration produced a 12% traffic increase but no evidence of an attendance effect, which is why no programme money is going into digital. The 2022 van averaged 11 attendances per visit and left no evaluation, which is why the plan does not scale outreach; the small minibus line brings groups to the building instead.

I used the staff interviews and the constraints as corroboration and as hard boundaries. JW and RS describe the 18:40 last bus, the £14 taxi and the failed 2023 minibus funding; AK describes the same barrier from a member's point of view; MD describes the childcare effect and the £180 session cost; PB describes the HVAC failure, the £18,000 quote and the 1 March expectation; LD describes the ageing craft group, the falling Film Club and the absence of Sunday data. The plan is built around those boundaries, not against them.

I checked the eight project journal entries. Two earlier notes were stale and are corrected here: the 2019 "east hall is climate-controlled" note (false since January 2025) and the "members want evening events" note (which reads the 44% "yes" without the 35% "no" or the stated-preference caveat). The journal's warning that the pack has no structural or floor-load data is also reflected: the 120/180 figures are audience capacities, not load ratings, and no heavy or suspended work is programmed without a building officer's check.

I used the 12 January 2026 updates over the seed pack wherever they conflict. The family fund is £4,000, not £9,000; the east hall repair is approved and scheduled, not merely an application; the Friday late bus exists, where the seed pack described only an 18:40 last service; the website update has no programme effect.

### 5.2 How the January updates changed my assumptions

The updates did not change the diagnosis; they changed what is testable and what is affordable.

**Family fund.** I had assumed that weekly childcare — 26 sessions at £180, or £4,680 — was affordable within the family fund. The update sets the fund at £4,000 and shows that even the full fund covers only 22 sessions (£3,960). I have planned 20 sessions (£3,600), held £400 for other family support, and built in six Saturdays without childcare. The family offer therefore changes from "childcare every week" to "childcare on 20 of 26 Saturdays, with the workshop still running every week". From April, the wording changes to "supported by the family fund". This is a material change: the Family Workshop remains the core, but childcare is now a limited enhancement rather than a weekly guarantee.

**East hall repair.** I had treated the east hall as uncertain and unavailable for the whole period. The update confirms the grant, the works dates (9–27 February), commissioning on 28 February and expected usability from 1 March. But the building officer says this is a plan, not a guarantee, and nothing should be booked before the commissioning certificate. I therefore did not schedule any east hall public events in January or February. I put the certificate check on 2 March, a soft opening on 14 March and the sensitive textile exhibition on 11 April, with two weeks of environmental monitoring and a curator sign-off before any textile is installed. The east hall changes from "maybe" to "planned, but gated".

**Transport.** I had assumed there was no viable evening offer, because the 2023 pilot ran with an 18:40 last bus. The update adds a Friday late bus from 6 February, last service 21:15, Fridays only, for six months, with a review in July and a ridership check after three months. I changed the evening plan from "no evening offer" to a Friday series ending at 20:30, and kept new Thursday evenings off. I did not extend the assumption to other weekdays, and I did not make core sessions depend on the bus. I added a 30 April data pack to feed the council's three-month review. The Friday series is therefore both a programme and an evidence-gathering exercise.

**Website.** The update says the migration is complete, online booking works and there is no programme effect. I have not allocated programme money to the website or a digital campaign, and I have not assumed that the 2024 traffic increase will translate into attendance.

### 5.3 What I am uncertain about

| Uncertainty | Why it matters | How the plan responds |
|---|---|---|
| **The cause of the decline** — transport, programming or changed habits | If transport is not the binding constraint, the Friday series may underperform; if programming is the issue, the east hall season may not be enough | The plan tests transport (Friday bus), adds programming (east hall, Friday talks, Sunday salons) and measures both. It does not claim to settle habits in six months; the final report will compare like-for-like months and state the limits of the evidence. |
| **The survey's stated preference** | 44% "yes" may not convert into attendance; 35% said no | The plan targets 25 per Friday event, not 44%; it counts actual attendance and bus use, and reports both to the board and the council. |
| **The 2023 pilot is a small, incomplete record** | Three nights, no written evaluation, unknown room and ticket income, and no-show rates that cannot be read as weak commitment because reservations may have been free | The Friday series changes the transport condition and records reservations, paid tickets and attendance separately. It is still a test, not a repeat of a proven format. |
| **The bus pilot's continuation** | If the council does not continue the bus after July, the Friday model may not survive | The plan covers January–June only and makes no July commitments. The Friday series is not a core session. If the bus ends, the remaining films can move to a Saturday afternoon or an early Friday slot, and the core still runs. |
| **The HVAC certificate date and environmental stability** | The textile exhibition could be delayed, or the hall could be certified but not stable enough for sensitive material | The certificate is a gate, not an assumption. Temperature and humidity are monitored for at least two weeks before any textile is installed, and the curator signs off. If the hall is not ready or not stable, the textile exhibition is postponed or replaced by a robust-material exhibition; it is not moved to the west hall, which has never been climate-controlled. No textiles are stored in the basement. |
| **Light and blackout** | The pack does not record blackout in either hall, and textiles are light-sensitive as well as humidity-sensitive | The Friday films and Film Club run in the evening, so they do not depend on blackout. The Sunday salons are talk, craft and performance, not film. The curator specifies light levels and cases for the exhibition, and any item that needs blackout and cannot be protected is excluded. |
| **Structural and floor-load data** | The pack has no floor-loading, rigging, access or fire-safety data; the 120/180 figures are audience capacities, not load ratings | No heavy, suspended or high-load installation is programmed without a building officer's check. The exhibition is designed as a light-installation textile show; a robust-material fallback that includes heavy sculpture would be subject to the same check. |
| **The family fund trustees' decision** | The £400 balance may be used elsewhere; the 20 sessions are a request, not a guarantee | Six no-childcare Saturdays are built into the schedule; the Family Workshop still runs. If the fund is reduced, childcare is reduced first, not the workshop. If 22 sessions are confirmed, two dates are restored. |
| **Attendance and materials estimates** | Craft 9, family 10, exhibition 350, Open House 150 and the other material counts are assumptions | The £5,125 contingency is the first call. Materials can be trimmed without cancelling sessions; attendance is reviewed monthly. |
| **Staff and volunteer capacity** | 2.0 FTE plus 0.5 FTE is a small team for a weekly Friday and Saturday programme plus an exhibition | Friday evenings use two paid sessional staff; no new permanent posts are created; volunteers are never alone after 18:00. If the rota becomes unsafe, Friday frequency is reduced before core sessions. |
| **The Thursday Film Club's decline** | The club fell 22% in 2025 and has no late transport; keeping it may not reverse that | It is retained for its existing local audience, not expanded, and reviewed if monthly attendance falls below 12 for three consecutive months. The Friday series, not the Thursday club, is the transport test. |
| **Sunday afternoon demand** | Only 12% prefer Sunday afternoon and there is no local evidence; the test may not recruit | Three sessions with a stop rule: if the first two average below 15, the third is cancelled and the budget returns to the reserve. |
| **Income** | Ticket and café income may be lower than hoped | The budget is gross and does not depend on income. Income is monitored monthly and reported separately. |
| **Seasonality and weather** | January and February are low months; half-term, Easter and late June affect families | Childcare-free Saturdays are placed on likely low dates (post-Christmas, half-term, Easter, late June); the final report compares with the same months in 2025. |
| **Cost assumptions** | Curator and evaluation day rates, daytime minibus hire and the extra campaign marketing are plan assumptions, not pack quotes | They are flagged in 4.5; the contingency and reserve absorb modest variance, and the treasurer will confirm VAT and rates before contracts. |

### 5.4 Why this mix, not a single bet

The board has three explanations and no decision. The evidence does not justify betting the whole £60,000 on one of them. The plan weights the budget toward what is already working (the core programme, including the Family Workshop, £18,900), a controlled transport test (Friday, £10,200), a signature programming season (east hall, £11,100, plus the Open House and commissions), and a small Sunday test (£1,260). Access transport, marketing and evaluation make up the rest.

The core is funded by the trust's programming budget, not a single external funder. The family fund only adds childcare; the bus is transport, not programme funding; the east hall repair is capital, not programming. If the Friday test fails, the core still runs. If the family fund is cut, the workshop still runs. If the east hall certificate slips, the west hall programme still runs. If the bus ends, the Friday films can move to a Saturday afternoon or an early Friday slot. That is the point of the portfolio: it gives the board evidence without putting the core programme at risk.

I considered moving the Thursday Film Club to a daytime matinee, to reach the 24% who prefer weekday morning. I did not do so, for three reasons: the pack gives no evidence of a daytime film audience; blackout is not recorded in either hall, and a daytime screening needs it; and the existing club has a local evening audience that a move could lose. The daytime gap is tested instead by the Sunday salons, which need no blackout, and by the existing Tuesday and Saturday morning sessions. If the board wants a weekday-morning film test, it can be added from the reserve after a blackout check.

---

## 6. How we will know whether it is working

The board's sixth open question is how to measure success. Gross attendance alone would reward activity rather than reach, so the plan uses a small dashboard. Targets are planning targets, not forecasts.

| Measure | Baseline | Target or decision rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Craft Group monthly attendance** | 2025 January–June average: 30.5 per month | 32 per month by June |
| **Thursday Film Club monthly attendance** | 2025 average: 17 per month | Stabilise at 17; if below 12 for three consecutive months, review and fold into the Friday programme or stop |
| **Family Workshop monthly attendance** | 2025 January–June average: 39.7 per month | 42 per month by June; childcare delivered on 20 dates |
| **Friday attendance** | New | 25 per event average; 30% arriving by bus; after the first 13 events (8 May), if below 20 per event or below 20% bus use, June reduces to monthly |
| **East hall exhibition** | New | 500 visitors and 350 workshop participants; curator environmental sign-off before any textile is installed |
| **Sunday salons** | New; survey preference 12% | 20 per session; if the first two average below 15, cancel the third |
| **New member households** | 610 members | 60 new households by June |
| **Repeat attendance** | Not currently measured | 25% of Friday and Sunday attenders return at least once |
| **Access** | 6 minibus runs | At least 8 passengers per run; if below 8 for three runs, stop and reallocate |
| **Income** | Not assumed | Ticket, workshop and café income reported monthly; the budget does not depend on it |
| **Staffing and licensing** | Current arrangements | Two paid staff at every evening event; no volunteer alone after 18:00; building empty by 23:30 |

**Reporting**

- **Monthly:** a one-page dashboard to the director and treasurer: attendance, income, bus counts, materials spend and any staffing issues.
- **End March:** a short board update on the Friday launch, the east hall certificate and the family-fund position.
- **30 April:** the transport data pack to the town council for its three-month review, covering ridership, attendance, reservations and no-shows.
- **Early May:** the Friday decision for June, using the stop rule above.
- **End June:** a board update and draft findings.
- **10 July:** the final evaluation report: what worked, what did not, and what the board should continue, change or stop.

---

## 7. Approval requested

The board is asked to:

1. **Approve the programme and the budget of £56,375**, including the £5,125 contingency and within the £60,000 ceiling, and note the £3,625 board reserve.
2. **Confirm the family-fund request** of 20 sessions at £180 (£3,600), with £400 held for other family support. If the trustees prefer to commit 22 sessions, the plan will restore childcare on 14 February and 28 March.
3. **Note the east hall certificate gate.** No east hall public event will be booked before the commissioning certificate; the 14 March soft opening and the 11 April exhibition are contingent on it, and the textile exhibition also requires two weeks of monitoring and curator sign-off.
4. **Agree the stop rules** for the Friday series, the Sunday salons, the Thursday Film Club and the minibus runs, so that underused activity can be stopped and the budget returned to the reserve without a further board decision.
5. **Agree the evaluation framework and reporting dates**, including the 30 April transport data pack and the 10 July final report.

# Harrowgate Community Trust

## Six-Month Programme Plan: January–June 2026

**Prepared for:** the Board of Trustees  
**Date:** January 2026, revised against the 12 January 2026 update pack  
**Programming budget:** £60,000  
**Status:** for approval

---

## 1. Summary

This is a portfolio plan, not a single bet. It protects the session that is working, tests the transport explanation on the one evening when transport has changed, uses the east hall only after it is certified, and keeps a small, honest test of the one slot on which the trust has no local evidence.

1. **Protect the Saturday family workshop.** It is the only session that grew in 2025 (+21%). It runs every Saturday. Family-fund childcare is requested for 20 of the 26 Saturdays, within the reduced £4,000 fund.
2. **Test transport on Fridays.** The town council's late bus starts on Friday 6 February and leaves the square at 21:15. The Friday series ends at 20:30, leaving 45 minutes to reach it. This is a bounded test with a stop rule, not a six-month commitment.
3. **Use the east hall after the certificate.** There is no public event in the east hall before the commissioning certificate. A soft opening follows the certificate, then a four-week textile exhibition from 11 April, subject to two weeks of environmental monitoring and curator sign-off.
4. **Test Sunday afternoon small.** Three salons, with a stop rule, because 12% of survey respondents prefer Sunday afternoon and the trust has no local evidence either way.
5. **Hold a reserve.** The plan commits £56,375, including a 10% contingency, and leaves £3,625 as a board reserve within the £60,000 ceiling.

| Headline | Number |
|---|---:|
| Tuesday Craft Group sessions | 25 |
| Thursday Film Club screenings | 12 |
| Saturday Family Workshops | 26 |
| Friday evening events | 20 |
| East hall public workshops | 10 |
| Sunday afternoon salons | 3 |
| Community-group minibus visits | 4 |
| Saturday family minibus runs | 2 |
| **Direct programme** | **£51,250** |
| **Contingency (10%)** | **£5,125** |
| **Total committed** | **£56,375** |
| **Board reserve to £60,000** | **£3,625** |

**Key dates**

| Date | Milestone |
|---|---|
| Fri 6 Feb | Friday late bus starts; Friday evening series launches |
| Mon 9–Fri 27 Feb | East hall HVAC works; no public events in the east hall |
| Sat 28 Feb | Commissioning scheduled |
| Mon 2 Mar | Commissioning certificate check; no east hall booking before this |
| Sat 14 Mar | East hall soft opening, subject to the certificate |
| Mon 16 Mar–Fri 3 Apr | Exhibition install and environmental monitoring; curator sign-off by 3 April |
| Sat 11 Apr–Sat 9 May | *Threads of Harrowgate* exhibition |
| Thu 30 Apr | Transport data pack to the town council |
| Early May | Friday series decision for June |
| Sat 20 Jun | Harrowgate Open House |
| Fri 10 Jul | Final evaluation report to the board |

---

## 2. What the evidence says

### 2.1 Attendance: a modest overall decline, but a clear mix shift

The attendance CSV is the only continuous quantitative series in the pack. It shows a 3.2% fall in total attendances in 2025 (1,030 to 997), but the fall is not uniform.

| Session | 2024 average per month | 2025 average per month | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Tuesday Craft Group | 33.9 | 29.2 | −14% |
| Thursday Film Club | 20.7 | 16.2 | −22% |
| Saturday Family Workshop | 31.2 | 37.8 | +21% |
| **All sessions** | **85.8** | **83.1** | **−3.2%** |

Two further points matter:

- **The decline is concentrated in the second half of 2025.** January–June 2025 totalled 523 attendances against 515 in the same months of 2024 (+1.6%). July–December 2025 totalled 474 against 515 (−8.0%).
- **The family workshop grew when childcare was added.** Its 2024 average was 26.9 in January–August and 42.3 in October–December, after the childcare pilot began. The 2025 January–June average was 39.7.

The implication is not that the whole programme is failing. It is that the weekday and evening offer is losing people while the Saturday family offer is working. The plan therefore protects the family workshop and treats the weekday and evening offer as the part that needs testing.

### 2.2 The survey: transport is the strongest signal, but it is a stated preference

The 2025 member survey had 240 responses from 610 members (39%). It was self-selected, and the survey volunteer's method note is explicit: the evening-transport figure is a stated preference; people were asked to imagine a bus, not tested on whether they would come, and were not asked what they would pay.

| Survey question | Result |
|---|---|
| What stops you attending more often? (up to two) | Transport 61%; programme does not appeal 34%; cost 29%; caring responsibilities 27%; other 11% |
| Would you attend an evening event if transport were available? | Yes 44%; maybe 21%; no 35% |
| Which time suits you best? | Saturday morning 38%; weekday morning 24%; weekday evening 18%; Sunday afternoon 12%; no preference 8% |
| Would free childcare make it easier to attend? | Yes 27%, of whom 81% are members with children under 12 |

Transport is the strongest signal, but 35% say they would not come even with transport, and the 44% is not a forecast. The time-preference data is more useful for scheduling: Saturday morning is the strongest preference, weekday morning is next, and Sunday afternoon is the weakest. That is why the plan is weighted to Saturday morning and daytime, and why the Sunday test is deliberately small.

The survey also explains why the plan does not put money into a digital campaign. Cost (29%) and caring responsibilities (27%) are addressed through pay-what-you-can pricing, free exhibition entry and the childcare offer, not through a separate subsidy line.

### 2.3 Prior interventions: remove friction, don't just change content

- **2023 Friday evening film pilot.** Three screenings drew 37, 23 and 19 people. Booking data shows 60 seats were reserved for the first night and 48 for the second, so attendance was 62% and 48% of reservations. The series was cancelled. The programmer's note says people liked the films but could not get home; the staff interviews corroborate the 18:40 last bus and a £14 return taxi. The mean attendance was 26.3, and the fall from first to third night was 49%. This is a strong hypothesis, not proof: only three nights, no written evaluation, the room is not recorded, and there is no ticket income data.
- **2024 Saturday childcare pilot.** Attendance rose from an average of 27 in the first eight months of 2024 to 42 in the last four. The family fund paid £180 per session. Staff report that families stayed for the café and some began attending the Tuesday Craft Group. This is the clearest evidence in the pack that removing a practical barrier works.
- **2024 website and ticketing migration.** Web traffic rose 12%, but there is no evidence that this changed attendance; the decline continued through 2025. Digital spend is therefore not treated as a solution.
- **2022 outreach van.** It averaged 11 attendances per visit, was withdrawn when its grant ended, and left no written evaluation. Staff remember it as "worthwhile but not a substitute for the building". It is not a model to scale.

### 2.4 Building, staffing and money are hard boundaries

- The east hall has not been climate-controlled since the HVAC unit failed in January 2025. The 2019 "climate-controlled" description is not relied on. The west hall and workshop room are usable throughout; the basement is damp and unsuitable for sensitive material.
- The pack contains no temperature or humidity readings for the east hall, before or after repair; no blackout data for either hall; and no floor-loading, rigging or fire-safety data. The 120 seated / 180 standing figures are audience capacities, not load ratings. Heavy or suspended work needs a building officer's check.
- The trust has 2.0 FTE permanent staff (director, programmer), 0.5 FTE administrator and eight volunteers. Evening events require two staff present; childcare requires two qualified workers; volunteers are not asked to work alone after 18:00.
- Events may run until 23:00, and the building must be empty by 23:30.
- The programming budget covers artists, materials, marketing, bought-in staff hours and event costs. Building repairs are funded separately. The family fund is separate and capped at £4,000 for this period.

The plan is built around these boundaries: no east hall public events before the certificate; no new Thursday evening series; Friday events end at 20:30; sessional staff cover evenings; no new permanent posts.

### 2.5 What the January updates changed

| Update | What it says | What I had assumed from the seed pack | What the plan now does |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Family fund** | £4,000 for January–June 2026, not the £9,000 in the seed pack. At £180 per Saturday, the fund covers at most 22 sessions (£3,960), leaving four Saturdays without family-fund support. The fund may also be used for other family support. From April, childcare must be advertised as "supported by the family fund" and cannot be described as permanently free. | I had assumed weekly childcare (26 × £180 = £4,680) was affordable. It is not. | I request 20 sessions (£3,600) and hold £400 for other family support, so six Saturdays run without childcare. The Family Workshop still runs every Saturday. From April, all childcare publicity uses the required wording. If the trustees confirm 22 sessions, I restore childcare on 14 February and 28 March. |
| **East hall repair** | The council has approved the capital grant. The contractor works 9–27 February; commissioning is 28 February; the hall is expected to be usable for sensitive material from 1 March. The building officer says this is a plan, not a guarantee, and nothing should be booked before the commissioning certificate. The repair is capital and outside the £60,000. | I had treated the east hall as uncertain and unavailable for the whole period. | I plan a certificate check on 2 March, a soft opening on 14 March and a textile exhibition from 11 April, subject to two weeks of monitoring and curator sign-off. No east hall events are scheduled in January or February. The £18,000 repair is excluded from the programming budget. |
| **Transport** | The town council has approved a Friday late bus pilot from 6 February 2026. The last service from the square will leave at 21:15 instead of 18:40. It is funded for six months, covers Fridays only, and will be reviewed in July; the council will look at ridership after three months. There is no change to Saturday or Sunday service and no extra service on other weekdays. | I had assumed no viable evening offer, because the 2023 pilot ran with an 18:40 last bus. | I plan a Friday series ending at 20:30, and no new Thursday evening series. I have not assumed late transport on any other day. The Friday series is a test, not a core commitment, and a data pack goes to the council by 30 April. |
| **Website** | The migration is complete, the old domain redirects, online booking works and the newsletter open rate is stable. The update says it has no effect on the programme plan. | I had treated the 2024 traffic increase as a possible attendance lever, but the evidence did not support that. | No programme money is allocated to the website or a digital campaign, and I have not assumed the 2024 traffic increase will translate into attendance. |

Two earlier project notes are now stale and are not relied on. The note "East hall is climate-controlled" comes from the 2019 building survey; the HVAC failed in January 2025 and the hall is uncontrolled until the repair is commissioned. The note "Members want evening events" reads the 44% "yes" without the 35% "no" or the survey volunteer's warning that the question was hypothetical. Both are corrected in this plan.

## 5. Rationale

### 5.1 Evidence I relied on

I treated the attendance CSV as the primary quantitative evidence because it is the only continuous series in the pack. It shows a 3.2% fall in total attendances in 2025, but the fall is not uniform: January–June 2025 was 1.6% above the same months of 2024, while July–December was 8.0% below; Craft Group fell 14%, the Film Club fell 22%, and the Saturday Family Workshop grew 21%. That is why the plan protects the Family Workshop and treats the weekday and evening offer as the part that needs testing, rather than assuming a general collapse.

I used the 2025 member survey as a signal, not a forecast. Transport is the most cited barrier at 61%, but the 44% who said they would attend an evening event if transport were available were answering a hypothetical question; the survey volunteer explicitly warns that the trust did not test whether they would actually come or what they would pay. I therefore did not plan on 44% turning up. I used the time-preference data — Saturday morning 38%, weekday morning 24%, weekday evening 18%, Sunday afternoon 12% — to weight the programme toward Saturday morning and daytime, and to keep the Sunday test small. Cost (29%) and caring responsibilities (27%) are addressed through pay-what-you-can pricing, free exhibition entry and the childcare offer, rather than through a separate subsidy line.

I used the prior interventions as natural experiments. The 2023 Friday films drew 37, 23 and 19 people, with 60 and 48 seats reserved, and were cancelled; the programmer's note and the staff interviews point to the journey home, with the 18:40 last bus and the £14 return taxi. That is a strong hypothesis, not proof, so the Friday series is a test with a stop rule. The 2024 childcare pilot, where the Family Workshop average rose from 27 to 42, is the clearest evidence that removing a practical barrier works; it is why childcare remains central to the family offer, within the reduced fund. The 2024 website migration produced a 12% traffic increase but no evidence of an attendance effect, which is why no programme money is going into digital. The 2022 van averaged 11 attendances per visit and left no evaluation, which is why the plan does not scale outreach; the small minibus line brings groups to the building instead.

I used the staff interviews and the constraints as corroboration and as hard boundaries. JW and RS describe the 18:40 last bus, the £14 taxi and the failed 2023 minibus funding; AK describes the same barrier from a member's point of view; MD describes the childcare effect and the £180 session cost; PB describes the HVAC failure, the £18,000 quote and the 1 March expectation; LD describes the ageing craft group, the falling Film Club and the absence of Sunday data. The plan is built around those boundaries, not against them.

I checked the eight project journal entries. Two earlier notes were stale and are corrected here: the 2019 "east hall is climate-controlled" note (false since January 2025) and the "members want evening events" note (which reads the 44% "yes" without the 35% "no" or the stated-preference caveat). The journal's warning that the pack has no structural or floor-load data is also reflected: the 120/180 figures are audience capacities, not load ratings, and no heavy or suspended work is programmed without a building officer's check.

I used the 12 January 2026 updates over the seed pack wherever they conflict. The family fund is £4,000, not £9,000; the east hall repair is approved and scheduled, not merely an application; the Friday late bus exists, where the seed pack described only an 18:40 last service; the website update has no programme effect.

### 5.2 How the January updates changed my assumptions

The updates did not change the diagnosis; they changed what is testable and what is affordable.

**Family fund.** I had assumed that weekly childcare — 26 sessions at £180, or £4,680 — was affordable within the family fund. The update sets the fund at £4,000 and shows that even the full fund covers only 22 sessions (£3,960). I have planned 20 sessions (£3,600), held £400 for other family support, and built in six Saturdays without childcare. The family offer therefore changes from "childcare every week" to "childcare on 20 of 26 Saturdays, with the workshop still running every week". From April, the wording changes to "supported by the family fund". This is a material change: the Family Workshop remains the core, but childcare is now a limited enhancement rather than a weekly guarantee.

**East hall repair.** I had treated the east hall as uncertain and unavailable for the whole period. The update confirms the grant, the works dates (9–27 February), commissioning on 28 February and expected usability from 1 March. But the building officer says this is a plan, not a guarantee, and nothing should be booked before the commissioning certificate. I therefore did not schedule any east hall public events in January or February. I put the certificate check on 2 March, a soft opening on 14 March and the sensitive textile exhibition on 11 April, with two weeks of environmental monitoring and a curator sign-off before any textile is installed. The east hall changes from "maybe" to "planned, but gated".

**Transport.** I had assumed there was no viable evening offer, because the 2023 pilot ran with an 18:40 last bus. The update adds a Friday late bus from 6 February, last service 21:15, Fridays only, for six months, with a review in July and a ridership check after three months. I changed the evening plan from "no evening offer" to a Friday series ending at 20:30, and kept new Thursday evenings off. I did not extend the assumption to other weekdays, and I did not make core sessions depend on the bus. I added a 30 April data pack to feed the council's three-month review. The Friday series is therefore both a programme and an evidence-gathering exercise.

**Website.** The update says the migration is complete, online booking works and there is no programme effect. I have not allocated programme money to the website or a digital campaign, and I have not assumed that the 2024 traffic increase will translate into attendance.

### 5.3 What I am uncertain about

| Uncertainty | Why it matters | How the plan responds |
|---|---|---|
| **The cause of the decline** — transport, programming or changed habits | If transport is not the binding constraint, the Friday series may underperform; if programming is the issue, the east hall season may not be enough | The plan tests transport (Friday bus), adds programming (east hall, Friday talks, Sunday salons) and measures both. It does not claim to settle habits in six months; the final report will compare like-for-like months and state the limits of the evidence. |
| **The survey's stated preference** | 44% "yes" may not convert into attendance; 35% said no | The plan targets 25 per Friday event, not 44%; it counts actual attendance and bus use, and reports both to the board and the council. |
| **The 2023 pilot is a small, incomplete record** | Three nights, no written evaluation, unknown room and ticket income, and no-show rates that cannot be read as weak commitment because reservations may have been free | The Friday series changes the transport condition and records reservations, paid tickets and attendance separately. It is still a test, not a repeat of a proven format. |
| **The bus pilot's continuation** | If the council does not continue the bus after July, the Friday model may not survive | The plan covers January–June only and makes no July commitments. The Friday series is not a core session. If the bus ends, the remaining films can move to a Saturday afternoon or an early Friday slot, and the core still runs. |
| **The HVAC certificate date and environmental stability** | The textile exhibition could be delayed, or the hall could be certified but not stable enough for sensitive material | The certificate is a gate, not an assumption. Temperature and humidity are monitored for at least two weeks before any textile is installed, and the curator signs off. If the hall is not ready or not stable, the textile exhibition is postponed or replaced by a robust-material exhibition; it is not moved to the west hall, which has never been climate-controlled. No textiles are stored in the basement. |
| **Light and blackout** | The pack does not record blackout in either hall, and textiles are light-sensitive as well as humidity-sensitive | The Friday films and Film Club run in the evening, so they do not depend on blackout. The Sunday salons are talk, craft and performance, not film. The curator specifies light levels and cases for the exhibition, and any item that needs blackout and cannot be protected is excluded. |
| **Structural and floor-load data** | The pack has no floor-loading, rigging, access or fire-safety data; the 120/180 figures are audience capacities, not load ratings | No heavy, suspended or high-load installation is programmed without a building officer's check. The exhibition is designed as a light-installation textile show; a robust-material fallback that includes heavy sculpture would be subject to the same check. |
| **The family fund trustees' decision** | The £400 balance may be used elsewhere; the 20 sessions are a request, not a guarantee | Six no-childcare Saturdays are built into the schedule; the Family Workshop still runs. If the fund is reduced, childcare is reduced first, not the workshop. If 22 sessions are confirmed, two dates are restored. |
| **Attendance and materials estimates** | Craft 9, family 10, exhibition 350, Open House 150 and the other material counts are assumptions | The £5,125 contingency is the first call. Materials can be trimmed without cancelling sessions; attendance is reviewed monthly. |
| **Staff and volunteer capacity** | 2.0 FTE plus 0.5 FTE is a small team for a weekly Friday and Saturday programme plus an exhibition | Friday evenings use two paid sessional staff; no new permanent posts are created; volunteers are never alone after 18:00. If the rota becomes unsafe, Friday frequency is reduced before core sessions. |
| **The Thursday Film Club's decline** | The club fell 22% in 2025 and has no late transport; keeping it may not reverse that | It is retained for its existing local audience, not expanded, and reviewed if monthly attendance falls below 12 for three consecutive months. The Friday series, not the Thursday club, is the transport test. |
| **Sunday afternoon demand** | Only 12% prefer Sunday afternoon and there is no local evidence; the test may not recruit | Three sessions with a stop rule: if the first two average below 15, the third is cancelled and the budget returns to the reserve. |
| **Income** | Ticket and café income may be lower than hoped | The budget is gross and does not depend on income. Income is monitored monthly and reported separately. |
| **Seasonality and weather** | January and February are low months; half-term, Easter and late June affect families | Childcare-free Saturdays are placed on likely low dates (post-Christmas, half-term, Easter, late June); the final report compares with the same months in 2025. |
| **Cost assumptions** | Curator and evaluation day rates, daytime minibus hire and the extra campaign marketing are plan assumptions, not pack quotes | They are flagged in 4.5; the contingency and reserve absorb modest variance, and the treasurer will confirm VAT and rates before contracts. |

### 5.4 Why this mix, not a single bet

The board has three explanations and no decision. The evidence does not justify betting the whole £60,000 on one of them. The plan weights the budget toward what is already working (the core programme, including the Family Workshop, £18,900), a controlled transport test (Friday, £10,200), a signature programming season (east hall, £11,100, plus the Open House and commissions), and a small Sunday test (£1,260). Access transport, marketing and evaluation make up the rest.

The core is funded by the trust's programming budget, not a single external funder. The family fund only adds childcare; the bus is transport, not programme funding; the east hall repair is capital, not programming. If the Friday test fails, the core still runs. If the family fund is cut, the workshop still runs. If the east hall certificate slips, the west hall programme still runs. If the bus ends, the Friday films can move to a Saturday afternoon or an early Friday slot. That is the point of the portfolio: it gives the board evidence without putting the core programme at risk.

I considered moving the Thursday Film Club to a daytime matinee, to reach the 24% who prefer weekday morning. I did not do so, for three reasons: the pack gives no evidence of a daytime film audience; blackout is not recorded in either hall, and a daytime screening needs it; and the existing club has a local evening audience that a move could lose. The daytime gap is tested instead by the Sunday salons, which need no blackout, and by the existing Tuesday and Saturday morning sessions. If the board wants a weekday-morning film test, it can be added from the reserve after a blackout check.

---

## 6. How we will know whether it is working

The board's sixth open question is how to measure success. Gross attendance alone would reward activity rather than reach, so the plan uses a small dashboard. Targets are planning targets, not forecasts.

| Measure | Baseline | Target or decision rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Craft Group monthly attendance** | 2025 January–June average: 30.5 per month | 32 per month by June |
| **Thursday Film Club monthly attendance** | 2025 average: 17 per month | Stabilise at 17; if below 12 for three consecutive months, review and fold into the Friday programme or stop |
| **Family Workshop monthly attendance** | 2025 January–June average: 39.7 per month | 42 per month by June; childcare delivered on 20 dates |
| **Friday attendance** | New | 25 per event average; 30% arriving by bus; after the first 13 events (8 May), if below 20 per event or below 20% bus use, June reduces to monthly |
| **East hall exhibition** | New | 500 visitors and 350 workshop participants; curator environmental sign-off before any textile is installed |
| **Sunday salons** | New; survey preference 12% | 20 per session; if the first two average below 15, cancel the third |
| **New member households** | 610 members | 60 new households by June |
| **Repeat attendance** | Not currently measured | 25% of Friday and Sunday attenders return at least once |
| **Access** | 6 minibus runs | At least 8 passengers per run; if below 8 for three runs, stop and reallocate |
| **Income** | Not assumed | Ticket, workshop and café income reported monthly; the budget does not depend on it |
| **Staffing and licensing** | Current arrangements | Two paid staff at every evening event; no volunteer alone after 18:00; building empty by 23:30 |

**Reporting**

- **Monthly:** a one-page dashboard to the director and treasurer: attendance, income, bus counts, materials spend and any staffing issues.
- **End March:** a short board update on the Friday launch, the east hall certificate and the family-fund position.
- **30 April:** the transport data pack to the town council for its three-month review, covering ridership, attendance, reservations and no-shows.
- **Early May:** the Friday decision for June, using the stop rule above.
- **End June:** a board update and draft findings.
- **10 July:** the final evaluation report: what worked, what did not, and what the board should continue, change or stop.

---

## 7. Approval requested

The board is asked to:

1. **Approve the programme and the budget of £56,375**, including the £5,125 contingency and within the £60,000 ceiling, and note the £3,625 board reserve.
2. **Confirm the family-fund request** of 20 sessions at £180 (£3,600), with £400 held for other family support. If the trustees prefer to commit 22 sessions, the plan will restore childcare on 14 February and 28 March.
3. **Note the east hall certificate gate.** No east hall public event will be booked before the commissioning certificate; the 14 March soft opening and the 11 April exhibition are contingent on it, and the textile exhibition also requires two weeks of monitoring and curator sign-off.
4. **Agree the stop rules** for the Friday series, the Sunday salons, the Thursday Film Club and the minibus runs, so that underused activity can be stopped and the budget returned to the reserve without a further board decision.
5. **Agree the evaluation framework and reporting dates**, including the 30 April transport data pack and the 10 July final report.

# Harrowgate Community Trust

## Six-Month Programme Plan: January–June 2026

**Prepared for:** the Board of Trustees  
**Date:** January 2026, revised against the 12 January 2026 update pack  
**Programming budget:** £60,000  
**Status:** for approval

---

## 1. Summary

This is a portfolio plan, not a single bet. It protects the session that is working, tests the transport explanation on the one evening when transport has changed, uses the east hall only after it is certified, and keeps a small, honest test of the one slot on which the trust has no local evidence.

1. **Protect the Saturday family workshop.** It is the only session that grew in 2025 (+21%). It runs every Saturday. Family-fund childcare is requested for 20 of the 26 Saturdays, within the reduced £4,000 fund.
2. **Test transport on Fridays.** The town council's late bus starts on Friday 6 February and leaves the square at 21:15. The Friday series ends at 20:30, leaving 45 minutes to reach it. This is a staged test with a stop rule, not an unconditional six-month commitment.
3. **Use the east hall after the certificate.** There is no public event in the east hall before the commissioning certificate. A soft opening follows the certificate, then a four-week textile exhibition from 11 April, subject to two weeks of environmental monitoring and curator sign-off.
4. **Test Sunday afternoon small.** Three salons, with a stop rule, because 12% of survey respondents prefer Sunday afternoon and the trust has no local evidence either way.
5. **Hold a reserve.** The plan commits £55,715, including a 10% contingency, and leaves £4,285 as a board reserve within the £60,000 ceiling.

---

## 2. What the evidence says

### 2.1 Attendance: a modest overall decline, but a clear mix shift

The attendance CSV is the only continuous quantitative series in the pack. It shows a 3.2% fall in total attendances in 2025 (1,030 to 997), but the fall is not uniform.

| Session | 2024 average per month | 2025 average per month | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Tuesday Craft Group | 33.9 | 29.2 | −14% |
| Thursday Film Club | 20.7 | 16.2 | −22% |
| Saturday Family Workshop | 31.2 | 37.8 | +21% |
| **All sessions** | **85.8** | **83.1** | **−3.2%** |

Two further points matter:

- **The decline is concentrated in the second half of 2025.** January–June 2025 totalled 523 attendances against 515 in the same months of 2024 (+1.6%). July–December 2025 totalled 474 against 515 (−8.0%).
- **The family workshop grew when childcare was added.** Its 2024 average was 26.9 in January–August and 42.3 in October–December, after the childcare pilot began. The 2025 January–June average was 39.7.

The implication is not that the whole programme is failing. It is that the weekday and evening offer is losing people while the Saturday family offer is working. The plan therefore protects the family workshop and treats the weekday and evening offer as the part that needs testing.

### 2.2 The survey: transport is the strongest signal, but it is a stated preference

The 2025 member survey had 240 responses from 610 members (39%). It was self-selected, and the survey volunteer's method note is explicit: the evening-transport figure is a stated preference; people were asked to imagine a bus, not tested on whether they would come, and were not asked what they would pay.

| Survey question | Result |
|---|---|
| What stops you attending more often? (up to two) | Transport 61%; programme does not appeal 34%; cost 29%; caring responsibilities 27%; other 11% |
| Would you attend an evening event if transport were available? | Yes 44%; maybe 21%; no 35% |
| Which time suits you best? | Saturday morning 38%; weekday morning 24%; weekday evening 18%; Sunday afternoon 12%; no preference 8% |
| Would free childcare make it easier to attend? | Yes 27%, of whom 81% are members with children under 12 |

Transport is the strongest signal, but 35% say they would not come even with transport, and the 44% is not a forecast. The time-preference data is more useful for scheduling: Saturday morning is the strongest preference, weekday morning is next, and Sunday afternoon is the weakest. That is why the plan is weighted to Saturday morning and daytime, and why the Sunday test is deliberately small.

The survey also explains why the plan does not put money into a digital campaign. Cost (29%) and caring responsibilities (27%) are addressed through pay-what-you-can pricing, free exhibition entry and the childcare offer, not through a separate subsidy line.

### 2.3 Prior interventions: remove friction, don't just change content

- **2023 Friday evening film pilot.** Three screenings drew 37, 23 and 19 people. Booking data shows 60 seats were reserved for the first night and 48 for the second, so attendance was 62% and 48% of reservations. The series was cancelled. The programmer's note says people liked the films but could not get home; the staff interviews corroborate the 18:40 last bus and a £14 return taxi. The mean attendance was 26.3, and the fall from first to third night was 49%. This is a strong hypothesis, not proof: only three nights, no written evaluation, the room is not recorded, and there is no ticket income data.
- **2024 Saturday childcare pilot.** Attendance rose from an average of 27 in the first eight months of 2024 to 42 in the last four. The family fund paid £180 per session. Staff report that families stayed for the café and some began attending the Tuesday Craft Group. This is the clearest evidence in the pack that removing a practical barrier works.
- **2024 website and ticketing migration.** Web traffic rose 12%, but there is no evidence that this changed attendance; the decline continued through 2025. Digital spend is therefore not treated as a solution.
- **2022 outreach van.** It averaged 11 attendances per visit, was withdrawn when its grant ended, and left no written evaluation. Staff remember it as "worthwhile but not a substitute for the building". It is not a model to scale.

### 2.4 Building, staffing and money are hard boundaries

- The east hall has not been climate-controlled since the HVAC unit failed in January 2025. The 2019 "climate-controlled" description is not relied on. The west hall and workshop room are usable throughout; the basement is damp and unsuitable for sensitive material.
- The pack contains no temperature or humidity readings for the east hall, before or after repair; no blackout data for either hall; and no floor-loading, rigging or fire-safety data. The 120 seated / 180 standing figures are audience capacities, not load ratings. Heavy or suspended work needs a building officer's check.
- The trust has 2.0 FTE permanent staff (director, programmer), 0.5 FTE administrator and eight volunteers. Evening events require two staff present; childcare requires two qualified workers; volunteers are not asked to work alone after 18:00.
- Events may run until 23:00, and the building must be empty by 23:30.
- The programming budget covers artists, materials, marketing, bought-in staff hours and event costs. Building repairs are funded separately. The family fund is separate and capped at £4,000 for this period.

The plan is built around these boundaries: no east hall public events before the certificate; no new Thursday evening series; Friday events end at 20:30; sessional staff cover evenings; no new permanent posts.

### 2.5 What the January updates changed

| Update | What it says | What I had assumed from the seed pack | What the plan now does |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Family fund** | £4,000 for January–June 2026, not the £9,000 in the seed pack. At £180 per Saturday, the fund covers at most 22 sessions (£3,960), leaving four Saturdays without family-fund support. The fund may also be used for other family support. From April, childcare must be advertised as "supported by the family fund" and cannot be described as permanently free. | I had assumed weekly childcare (26 × £180 = £4,680) was affordable under the seed pack's £9,000. It is not affordable within the £4,000 fund. | I request 20 sessions (£3,600) and hold £400 for other family support, so six Saturdays run without childcare. The Family Workshop still runs every Saturday. From April, all childcare publicity uses the required wording. If the trustees confirm 22 sessions, I restore childcare on 14 February and 28 March. |
| **East hall repair** | The council has approved the capital grant. The contractor works 9–27 February; commissioning is 28 February; the hall is expected to be usable for sensitive material from 1 March. The building officer says this is a plan, not a guarantee, and nothing should be booked before the commissioning certificate. The repair is capital and outside the £60,000. | I had treated the east hall as uncertain, with no firm date for sensitive use. | I plan a certificate check on 2 March, a soft opening on 14 March and a textile exhibition from 11 April, subject to two weeks of monitoring and curator sign-off. No east hall events are scheduled in January or February. The £18,000 repair is excluded from the programming budget. |
| **Transport** | The town council has approved a Friday late bus pilot from 6 February 2026. The last service from the square will leave at 21:15 instead of 18:40. It is funded for six months, covers Fridays only, and will be reviewed in July; the council will look at ridership after three months. There is no change to Saturday or Sunday service and no extra service on other weekdays. | I had assumed there was no viable new evening series, because the 2023 pilot ran with an 18:40 last bus. | I plan a Friday series ending at 20:30, and no new Thursday evening series. I have not assumed late transport on any other day. The Friday series is a test, not a core commitment, and a data pack goes to the council by 30 April. |
| **Website** | The migration is complete, the old domain redirects, online booking works and the newsletter open rate is stable. The update says it has no effect on the programme plan. | I had treated the 2024 traffic increase as a possible attendance lever, but the evidence did not support that. | No programme money is allocated to the website or a digital campaign, and I have not assumed the 2024 traffic increase will translate into attendance. |

Two earlier project notes are now stale and are not relied on. The note "East hall is climate-controlled" comes from the 2019 building survey; the HVAC failed in January 2025 and the hall is uncontrolled until the repair is commissioned. The note "Members want evening events" reads the 44% "yes" without the 35% "no" or the survey volunteer's warning that the question was hypothetical. Both are corrected in this plan.

Craft Group is in the workshop room. The Film Club, Family Workshop, Friday events and Sunday salons are in the west hall unless stated. The first four Friday events will measure the actual walk and connection time; if 45 minutes proves tight, the finish time moves earlier. Both evening offers have two people present: the Friday series uses the £220 sessional line, while the Thursday Film Club continues within the existing permanent-staff rota, with two staff present and no volunteer alone after 18:00. If the rota cannot cover a Thursday, that event is staffed from the contingency or cancelled rather than run with one person. There are no new Thursday evening events: the Thursday Film Club continues in its existing 19:00 slot for its existing local audience, and is not used as evidence that a new Thursday evening series would work. The east hall is not used for public events until the commissioning certificate is issued.

The plan is written against the 12 January update pack. January dates before 12 January are the existing programme continuing; they are included so the month is complete. January is for preparation and the existing programme; the new public elements start in February and later.
