April is the peak month because of exhibition install, commissions and the launch campaign. The monthly figures exclude family-fund childcare, which is outside the £60,000.

### 4.4 Outside the £60,000

**Family fund memorandum**

| Item | Detail |
|---|---:|
| Family fund available, January–June 2026 | £4,000 |
| Childcare: 20 Saturdays × £180 | £3,600 |
| Balance held for other family support | £400 |
| Saturdays with childcare | 20 of 26 |
| Saturdays without childcare | 6: 3 January, 14 February, 28 March, 4 April, 23 May, 27 June |

The January update says the fund could cover 22 sessions (£3,960). I request 20 sessions and hold £400, because the trustees warned that the fund may also be used for other family support and should not be assumed to be exclusively available to the Saturday workshop. If the trustees confirm 22 sessions, I will restore childcare on 14 February and 28 March, leaving a £40 balance. From April, all childcare publicity says "supported by the family fund" and does not describe childcare as permanently free.

**East hall repair**

The HVAC repair is funded by the council capital grant. The building officer's working figure is £18,000. The contractor works 9–27 February; commissioning is scheduled for 28 February; the hall is expected to be usable for sensitive material from 1 March, subject to the commissioning certificate. This is a capital cost, not a programming cost, and is excluded from the £60,000. No east hall public event is booked before the certificate; no sensitive material is stored in the basement; no heavy or suspended work is programmed without a building officer's check.

**Friday late bus**

The bus is funded by the town council for its six-month pilot. No programming money is allocated to it, and the plan does not assume it continues beyond June. The Friday series is designed so that the core programme still runs if the bus is withdrawn.

**Combined envelope check**

Across the two envelopes, budgeted spend is £59,315 against £64,000 available (£55,715 programming plus £3,600 family fund; £60,000 plus £4,000 available). The two envelopes are separate and not fungible; the comparison is for information only.

### 4.5 Budget assumptions

- **Unit costs:** the standard rates are from `sources/spaces-and-costs.md`. Artist and workshop leader £250 per session; film licence £120; materials £6 per participant; marketing £600 per month; evening staffing £220 per event; childcare £180 per session; minibus £240 per run; technician £150 per event.
- **Core session leaders:** the core lines assume a bought-in leader at the pack rate for every session. This is a deliberate choice to protect quality and to avoid asking the permanent team to absorb a weekly Friday series on top of its existing load. If existing staff or volunteers lead some sessions, the released amount stays in the board reserve; it is not assumed as a saving.
- **Curator and evaluation day rates:** the pack quotes a per-session artist rate, not a day rate. I have used £250 per day as a planning assumption for the curator and evaluator, and flagged it here rather than presenting it as a pack quote.
- **Marketing:** the £600 per month base is the pack rate. The additional £1,200 exhibition campaign and £600 Open House campaign are plan assumptions, not pack quotes; they are included because both are signature public moments, and they are the first marketing lines to be reduced if the board prefers a lower profile.
- **Minibus:** the £240 quote is for one evening. The daytime community and family runs are assumed at the same rate; the operator will be asked to confirm before booking.
- **Materials counts:** craft 9 participants per session; Family Workshop 10; Friday participatory events 20; Sunday salons 20; east hall season 350 in total (100 at the soft opening and 250 across the 10 public workshops); Open House 150. If attendance is higher, materials draw on the contingency.
- **Exhibition display:** cases, labels and hanging are within the curator/lead artist line; if a specialist case or mount is required for a fragile item, it draws on the contingency. The materials line covers participant materials only.
- **Evening staffing:** £220 per event covers two paid staff for four hours (17:00–21:00), including setup and close. Volunteers may support but are never alone after 18:00. The Thursday Film Club is staffed within the existing permanent-staff rota; if that is not possible, it draws on the contingency or is cancelled rather than run with one person.
- **Gallery invigilation:** the exhibition's daytime opening (Tuesday–Saturday, 10:00–16:00) is covered by the existing front-of-house rota and daytime volunteers, with no additional invigilation line. If the rota cannot cover five days, the gallery opens four days rather than reducing the workshop programme.
- **Childcare:** £180 per session, two qualified workers for four hours, paid from the family fund, not the £60,000.
- **Contingency and reserve:** the contingency is 10% of direct costs. It is the first call for materials under-estimation, certificate delay or additional sessional cover. If it is not used, it returns to the board. The board reserve is held for demand-led additions or overruns beyond the contingency.
- **VAT and income:** figures are gross; VAT treatment will be confirmed by the treasurer. Ticket, workshop and café income is not netted off the budget, and no income is assumed in it.

---

## 5. Rationale

### 5.1 Evidence I relied on

I treated the attendance CSV as the primary quantitative evidence because it is the only continuous series in the pack. It shows a 3.2% fall in total attendances in 2025, but the fall is not uniform: January–June 2025 was 1.6% above the same months of 2024, while July–December was 8.0% below; Craft Group fell 14%, the Film Club fell 22%, and the Saturday Family Workshop grew 21%. That is why the plan protects the Family Workshop and treats the weekday and evening offer as the part that needs testing, rather than assuming a general collapse.

I used the 2025 member survey as a signal, not a forecast. Transport is the most cited barrier at 61%, but the 44% who said they would attend an evening event if transport were available were answering a hypothetical question; the survey volunteer explicitly warns that the trust did not test whether they would actually come or what they would pay. I therefore did not plan on 44% turning up. I used the time-preference data — Saturday morning 38%, weekday morning 24%, weekday evening 18%, Sunday afternoon 12% — to weight the programme toward Saturday morning and daytime, and to keep the Sunday test small. Cost (29%) and caring responsibilities (27%) are addressed through pay-what-you-can pricing, free exhibition entry and the childcare offer, rather than through a separate subsidy line.

I used the prior interventions as natural experiments. The 2023 Friday films drew 37, 23 and 19 people, with 60 and 48 seats reserved, and were cancelled; the programmer's note and the staff interviews point to the journey home, with the 18:40 last bus and the £14 return taxi. That is a strong hypothesis, not proof, so the Friday series is a test with a stop rule. The 2024 childcare pilot, where the Family Workshop average rose from 27 to 42, is the clearest evidence that removing a practical barrier works; it is why childcare remains central to the family offer, within the reduced fund. The 2024 website migration produced a 12% traffic increase but no evidence of an attendance effect, which is why no programme money is going into digital. The 2022 van averaged 11 attendances per visit and left no evaluation, which is why the plan does not scale outreach; the small minibus line brings groups to the building instead.

I used the staff interviews and the constraints as corroboration and as hard boundaries. JW and RS describe the 18:40 last bus, the £14 taxi and the failed 2023 minibus funding; AK describes the same barrier from a member's point of view; MD describes the childcare effect and the £180 session cost; PB describes the HVAC failure, the £18,000 quote and the 1 March expectation; LD describes the ageing craft group, the falling Film Club and the absence of Sunday data. The plan is built around those boundaries, not against them.

I checked the eight project journal entries. Two earlier notes were stale and are corrected here: the 2019 "east hall is climate-controlled" note (false since January 2025) and the "members want evening events" note (which reads the 44% "yes" without the 35% "no" or the stated-preference caveat). The journal's warning that the pack has no structural or floor-load data is also reflected: the 120/180 figures are audience capacities, not load ratings, and no heavy or suspended work is programmed without a building officer's check.

I used the 12 January 2026 updates over the seed pack wherever they conflict. The family fund is £4,000, not £9,000; the east hall repair is approved and scheduled, not merely an application; the Friday late bus exists, where the seed pack described only an 18:40 last service; the website update has no programme effect.

### 5.2 How the January updates changed my assumptions

The updates did not change the diagnosis; they changed what is testable and what is affordable.

**Family fund.** Under the seed pack's £9,000, weekly childcare — 26 sessions at £180, or £4,680 — looked affordable. The update sets the fund at £4,000 and shows that even the full fund covers only 22 sessions (£3,960). I have planned 20 sessions (£3,600), held £400 for other family support, and built in six Saturdays without childcare. The family offer therefore changes from "childcare every week" to "childcare on 20 of 26 Saturdays, with the workshop still running every week". From April, the wording changes to "supported by the family fund". This is a material change: the Family Workshop remains the core, but childcare is now a limited enhancement rather than a weekly guarantee.

**East hall repair.** I had treated the east hall as uncertain, with no firm date for sensitive use. The update confirms the grant, the works dates (9–27 February), commissioning on 28 February and expected usability from 1 March. But the building officer says this is a plan, not a guarantee, and nothing should be booked before the commissioning certificate. I therefore did not schedule any east hall public events in January or February. I put the certificate check on 2 March, a soft opening on 14 March and the sensitive textile exhibition on 11 April, with two weeks of environmental monitoring and a curator sign-off before any textile is installed. The east hall changes from "maybe" to "planned, but gated".

**Transport.** I had assumed there was no viable new evening series, because the 2023 pilot ran with an 18:40 last bus. The update adds a Friday late bus from 6 February, last service 21:15, Fridays only, for six months, with a review in July and a ridership check after three months. I changed the plan for a new evening series from "not viable" to a Friday series ending at 20:30, and kept new Thursday evenings off. I did not extend the assumption to other weekdays, and I did not make core sessions depend on the bus. I added a 30 April data pack to feed the council's three-month review. The Friday series is therefore both a programme and an evidence-gathering exercise.

The round-1 journal note recommended a 2–3 event test. The bus update changes the sample: the council will review ridership after three months, and 2–3 nights would not give it or the trust a reliable read. I have therefore staged the series — 13 events to 8 May, then the full June programme only if the 8 May review clears the stop rule; otherwise June reduces to monthly. That is a longer test than the journal proposed, but it is conditional, and the core does not depend on it.

**Website.** The update says the migration is complete, online booking works and there is no programme effect. I have not allocated programme money to the website or a digital campaign, and I have not assumed that the 2024 traffic increase will translate into attendance.

### 5.3 What I am uncertain about

| Uncertainty | Why it matters | How the plan responds |
|---|---|---|
| **The cause of the decline** — transport, programming or changed habits | If transport is not the binding constraint, the Friday series may underperform; if programming is the issue, the east hall season may not be enough | The plan tests transport (Friday bus), adds programming (east hall, Friday talks, Sunday salons) and measures both. It does not claim to settle habits in six months; the final report will compare like-for-like months and state the limits of the evidence. |
| **The survey's stated preference** | 44% "yes" may not convert into attendance; 35% said no | The plan targets 25 per Friday event, not 44%; it counts actual attendance and bus use, and reports both to the board and the council. |
| **The 2023 pilot is a small, incomplete record** | Three nights, no written evaluation, unknown room and ticket income, and no-show rates that cannot be read as weak commitment because reservations may have been free | The Friday series changes the transport condition and records reservations, paid tickets and attendance separately. It is still a test, not a repeat of a proven format. |
| **The bus pilot's continuation** | If the council does not continue the bus after July, the Friday model may not survive | The plan covers January–June only and makes no July commitments. The Friday series is not a core session. If the bus ends, the remaining films can move to an early Friday slot that finishes before the 18:40 bus, or to a Saturday afternoon after a blackout check, and the core still runs. |
| **The HVAC certificate date and environmental stability** | The textile exhibition could be delayed, or the hall could be certified but not stable enough for sensitive material | The certificate is a gate, not an assumption. Temperature and humidity are monitored for at least two weeks before any textile is installed, and the curator signs off. If the hall is not ready or not stable, the textile exhibition is postponed or replaced by a robust-material exhibition; it is not moved to the west hall, which has never been climate-controlled. No textiles are stored in the basement. |
| **Light and blackout** | The pack does not record blackout in either hall, and textiles are light-sensitive as well as humidity-sensitive | The Friday films and Film Club run in the evening, when daylight is lower, and the club has operated in the existing room through the summer; blackout will still be confirmed before the first summer screening. The Sunday salons are talk, craft and performance, not film. The curator specifies light levels and cases for the exhibition, and any item that needs blackout and cannot be protected is excluded. |
| **Structural and floor-load data** | The pack has no floor-loading, rigging, access or fire-safety data; the 120/180 figures are audience capacities, not load ratings | No heavy, suspended or high-load installation is programmed without a building officer's check. The exhibition is designed as a light-installation textile show; a robust-material fallback that includes heavy sculpture would be subject to the same check. |
| **Film licensing in the east hall** | The trust's current film licence may not automatically cover the east hall; a new room can require a variation | The director confirms with the licensing officer before the 10 April preview. If the east hall is not covered, the Friday films stay in the west hall and the east hall is used for talks and the exhibition only. |
| **The family fund trustees' decision** | The £400 balance may be used elsewhere; the 20 sessions are a request, not a guarantee | Six no-childcare Saturdays are built into the schedule; the Family Workshop still runs. If the fund is reduced, childcare is reduced first, not the workshop. If 22 sessions are confirmed, two dates are restored. |
| **Attendance and materials estimates** | Craft 9, family 10, exhibition 350, Open House 150 and the other material counts are assumptions | The £5,065 contingency is the first call. Materials can be trimmed without cancelling sessions; attendance is reviewed monthly. |
| **Staff and volunteer capacity** | 2.0 FTE plus 0.5 FTE is a small team for a weekly Friday and Saturday programme plus an exhibition | Friday evenings use two paid sessional staff; no new permanent posts are created; volunteers are never alone after 18:00. If the rota becomes unsafe, Friday frequency is reduced before core sessions. |
| **The Thursday Film Club's decline** | The club fell 22% in 2025 and has no late transport; keeping it may not reverse that | It is retained for its existing local audience, not expanded, and reviewed if monthly attendance falls below 12 for three consecutive months. The Friday series, not the Thursday club, is the transport test. |
| **Sunday afternoon demand** | Only 12% prefer Sunday afternoon and there is no local evidence; the test may not recruit | Three sessions with a stop rule: if the first two average below 15, the third is cancelled and the budget returns to the reserve. |
| **Income** | Ticket and café income may be lower than hoped | The budget is gross and does not depend on income. Income is monitored monthly and reported separately. |
| **Seasonality and weather** | January and February are low months; school breaks, Easter and late June affect families | Childcare-free Saturdays are spread across likely lower-attendance dates (post-Christmas, February, Easter, late May and late June); the final report compares with the same months in 2025. |
| **Cost assumptions** | Curator and evaluation day rates, daytime minibus hire and the extra campaign marketing are plan assumptions, not pack quotes | They are flagged in 4.5; the contingency and reserve absorb modest variance, and the treasurer will confirm VAT and rates before contracts. |

### 5.4 Why this mix, not a single bet

The board has three explanations and no decision. The evidence does not justify betting the whole £60,000 on one of them. The plan weights the budget toward what is already working (the core programme, including the Family Workshop, £18,900), a controlled transport test (Friday, £10,200), a signature programming season (east hall, £10,500, plus the Open House and commissions), and a small Sunday test (£1,260). Access transport, marketing and evaluation make up the rest.

The core is funded by the trust's programming budget, not a single external funder. The family fund only adds childcare; the bus is transport, not programme funding; the east hall repair is capital, not programming. If the Friday test fails, the core still runs. If the family fund is cut, the workshop still runs. If the east hall certificate slips, the west hall programme still runs. If the bus ends, the Friday films can move to an early Friday slot that finishes before the 18:40 bus, or to a Saturday afternoon after a blackout check. That is the point of the portfolio: it gives the board evidence without putting the core programme at risk.

I considered moving the Thursday Film Club to a daytime matinee, to reach the 24% who prefer weekday morning. I did not do so, for three reasons: the pack gives no evidence of a daytime film audience; blackout is not recorded in either hall, and a daytime screening needs it; and the existing club has a local evening audience that a move could lose. The daytime gap is tested instead by the Sunday salons, which need no blackout, and by the existing Tuesday and Saturday morning sessions. If the board wants a weekday-morning film test, it can be added from the reserve after a blackout check.

---

## 6. How we will know whether it is working

The board's sixth open question is how to measure success. Gross attendance alone would reward activity rather than reach, so the plan uses a small dashboard. Targets are planning targets, not forecasts.

| Measure | Baseline | Target or decision rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Craft Group monthly attendance** | 2025 January–June average: 30.5 per month | 32 per month by June |
| **Thursday Film Club monthly attendance** | 2025 average: 17 per month | Stabilise at 17; if below 12 for three consecutive months, review and fold into the Friday programme or stop |
| **Family Workshop monthly attendance** | 2025 January–June average: 39.7 per month | 42 per month by June; childcare delivered on 20 dates |
| **Friday attendance** | New | 25 per event average; 30% arriving by bus; after the first 13 events (8 May), if below 20 per event or below 20% bus use, June reduces to monthly |
| **East hall exhibition** | New | 500 visitors and 350 participants across the soft opening and public workshops; curator environmental sign-off before any textile is installed |
| **Sunday salons** | New; survey preference 12% | 20 per session; if the first two average below 15, cancel the third |
| **New member households** | 610 members | 60 new households by June |
| **Repeat attendance** | Not currently measured | 25% of Friday and Sunday attenders return at least once |
| **Access** | 6 minibus runs | At least 8 passengers per run; if below 8 for three runs, stop and reallocate |
| **Income** | Not assumed | Ticket, workshop and café income reported monthly; the budget does not depend on it |
| **Staffing and licensing** | Current arrangements | Two paid staff at every evening event; no volunteer alone after 18:00; building empty by 23:30 |

**Reporting**

- **Monthly:** a one-page dashboard to the director and treasurer: attendance, income, bus counts, materials spend and any staffing issues.
- **End March:** a short board update on the Friday launch, the east hall certificate and the family-fund position.
- **30 April:** the transport data pack to the town council for its three-month review, covering ridership, attendance, reservations and no-shows.
- **After 8 May:** the Friday decision for June, using the stop rule above.
- **End June:** a board update and draft findings.
- **10 July:** the final evaluation report: what worked, what did not, and what the board should continue, change or stop.

---

## 7. Approval requested

The board is asked to:

1. **Approve the programme and the budget of £55,715**, including the £5,065 contingency and within the £60,000 ceiling, and note the £4,285 board reserve.
2. **Confirm the family-fund request** of 20 sessions at £180 (£3,600), with £400 held for other family support. If the trustees prefer to commit 22 sessions, the plan will restore childcare on 14 February and 28 March.
3. **Note the east hall certificate gate.** No east hall public event will be booked before the commissioning certificate; the 14 March soft opening and the 11 April exhibition are contingent on it, and the textile exhibition also requires two weeks of monitoring and curator sign-off.
4. **Agree the stop rules** for the Friday series, the Sunday salons, the Thursday Film Club and the minibus runs, so that underused activity can be stopped and the budget returned to the reserve without a further board decision.
5. **Agree the evaluation framework and reporting dates**, including the 30 April transport data pack and the 10 July final report.

---

*Prepared from the current source pack and the four 12 January 2026 updates. The £18,000 HVAC repair, the family fund and the Friday bus are outside the £60,000 programming budget; ticket income is not netted against it.*

journalAfter.title: 2023 Friday film pilot failed as a series — do not repeat it without transport
journalAfter.body:
Conclusion: the pilot failed as a series and should not be repeated in its 2023 form. Attendance fell 37 → 23 → 19 across the three Friday nights (79 attendances in total, mean 26.3), a 49% drop from the first night to the third, and the series was cancelled. Reservations fell too, from 60 seats for the first night to 48 for the second, so this was not only a no-show problem: attendance was 62% of reservations on night one and 48% on night two. Measured against the purpose of building a recurring evening audience, it did not succeed.

Evidence: prior-interventions.md (2023 entry) gives the three attendances, the cancellation and the 60/48 bookings, plus the programmer's note that "people liked the films; the problem was getting home". staff-interviews.md: JW (front of house) says the last scheduled minibus leaves the square at 18:40, after which it is a £14 return taxi or a lift; RS (volunteer driver) says a minibus was quoted at £240 a night but driver funding fell through, so the pilot ran without one. The regular Thursday film club also fell from a 2024 average of 20.7 to 16.2 in 2025 (−22%), so film programming was already softening; the pilot's first night of 37 was above that routine average, which is the one positive demand signal in the record.

Why it should not be repeated: the pilot tested "Friday evening film with no way home", not "Friday evening film". A 2026 repeat with no transport, unpriced reservations and no measurement beyond door count would be expected to produce the same decline, and would again fail to tell the board whether the problem is the programme or the journey home.

Uncertainty: only three nights, and no written evaluation beyond one programmer's note. The room is not recorded; 60 first-night seats is consistent with the west hall's 60-seat capacity, but that is an inference. It is not recorded whether reservations were paid, so the 38% and 52% no-show rates cannot be read as evidence of weak commitment. No ticket income figures survive, so the pilot's unit economics are unknown.

journalAfter.title: East hall: HVAC failed January 2025; 1 March 2026 is conditional, not committed
journalAfter.body:
Conclusion: as of the October–November 2025 interviews, the east hall is open but not climate-controlled. The HVAC unit failed in January 2025 and cannot be run until it is repaired. The repair is quoted at £18,000 and is a capital grant application to the council, funded separately from the £60,000 programming budget. If the grant is approved, the repair is scheduled for late February 2026 and the hall would be usable from 1 March 2026. Until the repair is complete and commissioned, the hall is unavailable for any activity that needs stable temperature or humidity.

Evidence: constraints.md — the east hall is unavailable for activities needing stable temperature or humidity until the HVAC repair is complete and commissioned; the west hall and workshop room are usable throughout. staff-interviews.md, PB (building officer): the 2019 survey recorded climate control, "that is no longer true", the unit failed in January 2025, the quote is £18,000, the unit cannot run until repaired, a capital grant application is with the council, repair would be scheduled for late February 2026 and the hall usable from 1 March. spaces-and-costs.md: capacity 120 seated / 180 standing, internal with no hire fee, completion expected late February 2026. The 2019 "climate-controlled" description is out of date and must not be relied on for a textile exhibition; this corrects the earlier journal note "East hall is climate-controlled".

Uncertainty: 1 March is an earliest case, not a commitment. It depends on a grant decision that has not been made, on the works not slipping, and on commissioning. The pack contains no temperature or humidity readings for the hall, before or after repair, so the repaired hall's performance is unproven; logged readings should be taken before any sensitive material is committed. For January–February 2026 the plan must assume the hall has no climate control. The west hall (60 seated) has never been climate-controlled, the workshop room holds 24 and has no blackout, and the basement store is damp in winter, so there is no climate-safe fallback on site.

journalAfter.title: East hall can hold durable, non-sensitive material only until the HVAC is commissioned
journalAfter.body:
Conclusion: while the HVAC is down, the east hall can hold durable, non-sensitive material and events whose value does not depend on stable temperature or humidity — metal, stone, fired ceramics, glass, robust sculpture and construction, set/scenery, large props, equipment, market stalls, standing receptions, rehearsals, amplified performance and large meetings. Its 120 seated / 180 standing capacity makes it the only room that can hold an audience above 60.

It cannot hold, until the repair is commissioned and shown to work: textiles, costume, paper, books, archives, photographs, film stock, paintings and works on paper, leather, and instruments or other objects that need stable relative humidity. A textile exhibition is therefore not safe in the east hall before commissioning. Moving it to another room does not solve the problem: the west hall has never been climate-controlled, the workshop room holds 24 and has no blackout, and the basement store is damp in winter with no environmental control at all.

Evidence: constraints.md — east hall restriction; basement damp and unsuitable for sensitive material; west hall and workshop usable throughout. spaces-and-costs.md — east hall 120 seated / 180 standing, west hall 60 seated / 90 standing with no climate control, workshop room 24 with no blackout, café 40, basement store damp in winter. staff-interviews.md, PB — west hall never climate-controlled; basement damp with no environmental control; the east hall's 2019 "climate-controlled" status is no longer true. The existing journal note "East hall is climate-controlled" is a 2019 statement and is now false.

Uncertainty: the pack gives no actual temperature or relative-humidity figures, so the line between "robust" and "sensitive" is a professional judgement, not a measurement. The east hall's blackout is not recorded either way (only the workshop room is noted as having none), which matters for film or light-sensitive display. If the capital grant is delayed, the hall stays uncontrolled for the whole six months, and any programming that assumes otherwise would need a fallback.

journalAfter.title: A 2026 evening series is worth one bounded, transport-backed test — not a six-month commitment
journalAfter.body:
Conclusion: the evidence supports one bounded, transport-backed test of evening programming in 2026 — not a six-month evening series, and not a repeat of the 2023 design. The 2023 pilot is a negative result for an evening event without transport; it is not a verdict on evening events. The 2025 survey points the same way but is weaker than it looks: 61% name transport as a barrier, 44% say they would attend an evening event if transport were available, 21% maybe and 35% no. That is a stated preference — the survey volunteer's own method note says respondents were asked to imagine a bus, were not tested on whether they would come, and were not asked what they would pay. The only session that grew was the Saturday family workshop, so evening programming would be a test against the trend, not an extension of demonstrated demand.

A test worth running: a short run of 2–3 evening events in the first half of 2026, in the west hall (60) or the east hall from 1 March if the HVAC is commissioned (120), with a booked minibus, paid reservations, and a recorded comparison of reservations, actual attendance and no-shows. Marginal cost per film night with transport is £730 (£120 licence + £150 technician + £220 evening staffing + £240 minibus), before any share of the £600 monthly marketing. At the pilot's mean attendance of 26.3 that is £27.76 per attendee; at its best night of 37 it is £19.73. No ticket price or income data is in the pack, so the subsidy per seat is unknown: if a ticket were £8, break-even would need about 92 people, more than the west hall can seat and only possible in the repaired east hall. That argues for a short test, a cheaper format, or an explicit subsidy — not a long run.

A daytime comparator is also untested: LD (programmer) says there is no data on a Sunday afternoon series; 12% of survey respondents prefer Sunday afternoon, against 18% for weekday evening and 38% for Saturday morning. A Sunday afternoon event avoids the £240 minibus, and the pack's two-staff rule is specific to evenings, so it may also avoid the £220 evening staffing cost — but it answers a different question and should not be treated as evidence about evening demand.

Uncertainty: the survey figures are intentions, not behaviour, and the 35% "no" is a real constraint on the size of the evening audience. The pilot's room and ticket income are unknown; the pack does not record blackout in either hall; and demand may be for a particular film or format rather than for evening events in general. The test should be judged on paid attendance, not reservations or intentions. This also corrects the earlier journal note "Members want evening events", which reads the 44% as support without the 35% "no" or the stated-preference caveat.

journalAfter.title: East hall: no structural or floor-load data — climate suitability is not load approval
journalAfter.body:
Conclusion: the pack can answer what the east hall can hold only in climate terms. It contains no floor-loading, rigging, access or fire-safety data, so the companion note's list of durable material should not be read as approval for heavy sculpture, large set builds, suspended work or high-load installations. Those need a structural or technical check before they are programmed. A textile exhibition is primarily a humidity question; a sculpture or set build is primarily a structural one.

Evidence: spaces-and-costs.md gives capacity, hire cost and climate notes for the east hall but no structural data; staff-interviews.md (PB) discusses the HVAC and damp, not floor loading or rigging; constraints.md restricts climate-sensitive use and says nothing about load. The 120 seated / 180 standing figures are audience capacities, not load ratings.

Uncertainty: absence of data is not evidence that the floor is weak — it means the question is unanswered. The hall may well be capable of heavy work; the pack simply does not say. Any heavy or suspended installation should be referred to the building officer before it is costed into the plan.
